input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_title: Limitations: Dataset Scale, Domain Transfer, and Retrieval Dependence
input.section_summary: Explicitly discuss the stated limitations: small/curated dataset scale, challenges in transferring the workflow across domains, and sensitivity to retrieval quality. For each limitation, outline practical mitigations and short-term experiments (e.g., larger/diverse corpora, domain adaptation strategies, retrieval ensemble/robustness checks) that could be pursued within constrained resources.

output:
We conclude by articulating three primary limitations of the proposed graph-aware prompting workflow and by suggesting practical mitigations and short-term experiments that could be pursued within constrained resources.

\textbf{Dataset scale.} The empirical evaluation in this work is intentionally focused and uses a small, curated set of source materials; this limits the observable failure modes and the extent to which results can be generalized beyond the evaluated corpora (general background knowledge). To mitigate scale-related risks we recommend: (1) assembling a broader, heterogeneous corpus that spans multiple subdomains and publication venues; (2) performing controlled data-ablation studies that measure sensitivity to the amount and diversity of source documents; and (3) using lightweight data-augmentation strategies (for example, paraphrase- or snippet-level expansion) to increase the variety of retrieved evidence available to the generator. These are proposed experiments rather than claims about effectiveness and are intended to guide short-term validation efforts.

\textbf{Domain transfer.} The workflow components (section graphs, prompt templates, and retrieval queries) are engineered for the topical domains examined in our experiments and therefore may require adaptation when applied to substantially different subject areas (general background knowledge). Practical mitigations include modularizing templates and schema definitions so they can be retargeted with minimal editing, and evaluating simple domain-adaptation strategies such as: (a) seeding prompts with a small set of in-domain exemplars; (b) tuning retrieval-query heuristics per domain; and (c) exploring few-shot or adapter-based model updates where compute budgets permit. Short-term experiments to quantify transferability could measure generation and citation-fidelity metrics on held-out domains after applying each adaptation strategy.

\textbf{Retrieval dependence and evidence quality.} The end-to-end grounding of section text in external evidence depends on the recall and ranking quality of the retrieval subsystem; low-quality or missing evidence naturally constrains the ability to produce well-supported assertions (general background knowledge). To reduce sensitivity to single-retriever failure modes we propose: ensemble retrieval (combining complementary indexers and query formulations), explicit reranking and calibration steps before evidence injection, and conservative fallback behaviors that force the generator to emit qualifiers or to mark unsupported claims for human review. Empirical robustness checks that we recommend include ablations that perturb retrieved snippets, measuring the downstream change in unsupported-assertion counts, and stress tests that withhold key documents to observe failure modes.

Across these three areas, two cross-cutting practices improve reproducibility and auditability: (i) preserve machine-readable section outputs (the JSON schema used by the pipeline) and full provenance metadata for every injected snippet; and (ii) record prompt-and-retrieval seeds so experiments can be re-run deterministically where APIs permit. These practices reduce the effort required to trace and remediate errors regardless of the specific mitigation adopted.

Finally, we emphasize that the suggestions above are practical directions for further validation rather than definitive remedies. Given the limited scale of the present evaluation, prioritizing transparent, reproducible experiments (for example, data-ablation, cross-domain transfer tests, and retrieval-perturbation studies) will best inform which mitigations most effectively increase citation fidelity and reduce unsupported assertions in future work.
